answer_text:
Five upgrades in ResStock 2025 Release 1 are HVAC demand flexibility measures: upgrades 24–28. The upgrade list names them as HVAC Demand Flexibility with on-peak load shedding (2°F and 4°F offsets) and with pre-peak load shifting (4-hour at 2°F and 4°F, and 1-hour at 2°F). Upgrades 22–23 are EV demand flexibility measures, so they’re not HVAC. 
github

How they differ
Upgrade	Strategy	Offset	Event window
24	On-peak load shedding	2°F	4-hour on-peak
25	Pre-peak load shifting	2°F	4-hour pre-peak
26	On-peak load shedding	4°F	4-hour on-peak
27	Pre-peak load shifting	4°F	4-hour pre-peak
28	Pre-peak load shifting	2°F	1-hour pre-peak

Table parameters are from the measure documentation. In its final-parameter table, the shedding upgrades have no pre-peak period, and the shifting upgrades have no on-peak offset. The two strategies are not combined in any upgrade. 
nlr

Strategy (shed vs. shift)

Load shedding lowers the heating setpoint and raises the cooling setpoint during the on-peak window, so indoor temperature drifts and comfort is traded for lower peak load. 
nlr
Load shifting preheats (on heating days) or precools (on cooling days) during a pre-peak window, so less heating or cooling is needed on-peak. 
nlr
Shedding curtails load, and some of it may never be recovered. Shifting moves load to another time. The README says the same. 
s3

Offset size (2°F vs. 4°F)

This is the setpoint change magnitude. The 4°F cases produce larger peak reductions than the 2°F cases.
The documentation reports about a 57% average reduction in peak-period winter heating electricity and 54% in summer cooling for the 4°F, 4-hour-peak case across all 51 states. 
nlr
Per-scenario stock-level numbers appear only in the report’s figures, so I have not quoted them.

Pre-peak duration (4 hours vs. 1 hour)

This is how long the preconditioning runs. Upgrade 28 is the short-duration variant of upgrade 25 at the same 2°F offset.
Shared dispatch rules
Dispatch occurs every day in the dataset, far more often than real programs (historically 15–25 days per year), to estimate maximum technical potential. 
nlr
Daily-average temperature thresholds apply to shifting: precool only above 68°F, preheat only below 50°F. Shedding has no temperature threshold, so on shoulder days between 50°F and 68°F only shedding is dispatched. 
nlr
The on-peak period is the 4-hour window containing the peak, based on Cambium MidCase 2050 net load data by state and season. 
nlr
Heating setpoints can’t go below 55°F and cooling setpoints can’t go above 82°F. 
nlr
Each building’s start and stop times are randomly shifted by up to ±30 minutes to reduce coincident snapback. 
nlr
The measure applies to about 99.7% of dwellings, excluding those with neither heating nor cooling. 
nlr
The measure assumes every unit has a smart thermostat, and annualized energy or savings metrics should not be used directly. Splice baseline and upgrade daily profiles in the proportion you want. 
nlr
Discrepancy to resolve

The README summary I retrieved lists the shedding events as a “1-hour on-peak” window, and its narrative mentions “2-hr or 4-hr” pre-peak windows. That conflicts with the measure documentation, which uses a 4-hour on-peak window and 1- or 4-hour pre-peak windows. I’m treating the measure documentation as authoritative. The README came through an automated summary rather than a direct read, so please check the exact durations against the README’s table before citing them. That check is especially worth doing if you own this documentation.

The switchover is at 35°F outdoor air temperature, per the NLR measure documentation for the ResStock 2025 Release 1 Dual Fuel Heat Pump upgrade (White, Stenger, and Parker, NLR/TP-5500-96414, May 2026).

The document says the switchover temperature for this measure upgrade is set at 35°F, and that it is fixed for all dwellings. 
nlr

nlr
The temperature does not vary by region or climate zone. The two test dwellings, one in climate zone 6A (WI) and one in 2A (TX), both use 35°F. 
nlr
Savings are smaller in the Very Cold climate zone because fewer heating hours fall above 35°F, so the heat pump serves less of the load.

answer_text:
Short answer: Advanced air sealing applies to homes with a baseline infiltration of about 6 ACH50 or more. Those homes are sealed to 5 ACH50. The measure applies to roughly 92% of dwelling units.

Eligibility

The only eligibility criterion for the air sealing portion is infiltration rate. The NLR measure documentation (NLR/TP-5500-96281) says it applies to dwelling units with infiltration rates of ?6 ACH50 and does not apply to units below 6 ACH50. I found no housing-type or construction exclusions for air sealing.
The companion package report (NLR/TP-5500-96349) says the same: units at or above 6 ACH50 are eligible.
Boundary wording: 96281 is inconsistent on whether the cutoff is “?6” (Measure Summary, Sec. 1.2) or “above 6” (Sec. 1.3). This only matters for homes at exactly 6.0 ACH50. If it matters for your work, check the upgrade.infiltration_reduction logic in the ResStock code on GitHub.
The wall-type exclusions (already-insulated walls, non-wood-stud walls) apply only to the drill-and-fill insulation in upgrades 14 and 16, not to air sealing.

Leakage level

Eligible homes are sealed to 5 ACH50 (a fixed target, not a percent reduction). 96281 (Sec. 1.3) says units above the threshold “will receive advanced air sealing and then have an infiltration rate of 5 ACH50.”
96349 (Sec. 1.2) describes it as a goal of 5 ACH50. It says this reflects average infiltration in empirical studies across representative climate zones and avoids homes that already meet 2024 IECC.
96281 calls the target “very aggressive” and notes that reaching it may take more than traditional air sealing, such as over-cladding or window replacement.

Share of dwelling units

96281 reports about 92% of existing units in the Measure Summary and 92.2% of baseline dwelling units in Sec. 4.2. About 8% fall below 6 ACH50 and are excluded.
96349 gives no air-sealing-only percentage. Its 98% figure covers the whole four-measure package. Summing its Table 1 rows where air sealing is “YES” gives about 92.3%. That sum is my own arithmetic, not a stated figure.
The 92.2% in Table 3 of 96281 comes from a scenario filter (excluding uninsulated wood-stud walls). The report does not present it as an eligibility rule.

Caveats

I did not retrieve the standalone Upgrade 11 measure documentation. The upgrade measures page links to it, but my fetch was blocked. The numbers above come from the two NLR documents covering packages that include the same air sealing measure, and they agree with each other.
The upgrade measures page marks Upgrade 11 with an asterisk, meaning its documentation is not yet available, though it lists a link. Confirm that link before citing it.
All of these sources are NLR/DOE technical reports, not peer-reviewed journal articles.

Are you asking about the baseline ResStock sample (as in the 92% figure), or about a particular weighted subset such as a state, income group or housing type? The share would differ.

In ResStock 2025 Release 1, Geometry Stories has about 49–53% of housing units in one-story buildings, depending on which official document you read. The data source is EIA’s 2009 RECS microdata, and basements are not counted as stories.

Share of one-story units: two official sources disagree

The versioned 2025 Release 1 online documentation lists 1 story at 53% stock saturation, 2 stories at 33%, and 3 stories at 7.7%.
The ResStock 2025 Release 1 Technical Reference Guide (Table 11, Section 8.2) lists 1 story at 49%, 2 stories at 37%, and 3 stories at 8%.
The options beyond 4 stories (0.79% at 5, 0.7% at 6, and so on) match between the two.
I couldn’t tell from these sources which table is authoritative. The Technical Reference Guide is a draft dated October 2025, so it may carry numbers from a different iteration of the tsv.
The documentation values are generated from the characteristic files, so I’d lean toward 53%. I haven’t confirmed that.
To settle it, check Geometry Stories.tsv in the 2025_Release_1 tag of the ResStock GitHub repo, or compute the share from the build_existing_model.geometry_stories column in the OEDI baseline data. Both are weighted by the sampling weights.

Data source

Both documents give the source as the U.S. EIA 2009 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) microdata.
Single-family detached and attached units use the RECS STORIES field. Multifamily with 5+ units uses NUMFLRS.
All mobile homes are assigned 1 story.
The 2-unit and 3–4-unit buildings use the 5–9-unit multifamily distribution, capped at 4 stories, because RECS doesn’t report stories for them.

Basements

The Technical Reference Guide says the count of stories does not include basements but would include finished attics.
The documentation defines the argument geometry_num_floors_above_grade as floors above grade, with conditioned attics included.
That is consistent with basements being excluded.

Caveats

I read the Technical Reference Guide through a summarizing fetch tool, so the table values and the basements sentence should be checked against the PDF itself (Section 8.2, Tables 11–13).
The source is 2009 RECS data, so the distribution reflects that survey vintage.

The ResStock team recommends using at least 1,000 samples when nothing more specific is known.

The ResStock docs say uncertainty levels off around 1,000 samples, and that using fewer can give uncertainty too high for decisions or conclusions. 
github
Their convergence analysis tested quantities such as average annual site electricity use and peak magnitude. At about 1,000 samples, all of the tested quantities had roughly 15% uncertainty or less. 
github
The FAQ calls this a conservative reference that keeps sampling discrepancy at 15% or lower for many common quantities of interest, as described in the End-Use Load Profiles methodology report, section 5.1.3. 
github
1,000 is a floor, not a target. For a particular analysis, the team suggests estimating the standard error (standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample count) to set the appropriate minimum. 
github
If a geography has too few samples, the team recommends grouping nearby geographies together to increase sample size and reduce uncertainty. 
github
This applies to the samples in your analysis subset, not the total simulated. In the example, each of 550,000 sampled units represents about 242 real dwelling units, so 1,000 samples represents about 242,000.

Yes, the ResStock team documents this as a known issue. The only source I found is the team’s own issue report, “Wall Type Issue, Especially in Maine.” I did not find a GitHub issue or independent publication that corroborates it, so it is a single official source.

The problem

The Geometry Wall Type characteristic is wrong for Maine. The report gives the single-family detached stock as about 10% wood-framed, 12% brick and 78% concrete masonry (CMU). That does not match local knowledge or Vermont, which has a similar housing stock.
The report says it believes all published ResStock datasets are affected, and it cites 2024 Release 2 as an example, where Maine’s wood-framed share is the lowest of any state. It does not say whether the 2025 Release 1 values differ, so check that directly.
The cause is the Maine portion of the county tax assessor data that ResStock uses for wall type. The team spot-checked records against Zillow photos and found considerable mislabeling. Zillow imports the same assessor data, so it shows the same errors.
Other building types in Maine also show unexpected trends.
Maine is the confirmed case. The report says similar problems haven’t been seen elsewhere, but it hasn’t done a comprehensive check of other states.

What it affects

Wall Type and Wall Exterior Finish are directly affected. Insulation Wall is minimally affected.
Upgrade applicability can be affected. For example, insulation measures limited to wood-frame walls apply to fewer Maine dwelling units than they should.
The team does not currently believe there are significant impacts on energy consumption, emissions or energy bills, in either baseline or upgrade results.

What the report recommends if you need Maine wall type results

For wall type or exterior finish distributions, use ResStock results from nearby states, especially Vermont and New Hampshire.
For measures whose applicability depends on wall type, either reweight the Maine results using nearby-state wall type distributions, or use the nearby-state results directly.

Status

The report lists the status as “Current.” A preliminary investigation is done and a detailed one is pending. No fix has been implemented, and the report gives no timeline or linked GitHub issue.

Things I couldn’t confirm

Whether the Maine wall type values changed between 2024 Release 2 and 2025 Release 1, which is the dataset you would likely use now. Comparing in.geometry_wall_type for Maine and Vermont in both releases would settle it.
Whether an internal ticket or planned fix is tracked outside the public docs. You may know more than I can see on that.

Which release are you working with, and is this for a deliverable or a specific analysis? That would help me suggest whether reweighting or borrowing Vermont/New Hampshire results fits better.
